in_scope_clauses.summary:
No data, no market — substances ≥1 tonne/year per manufacturer
or importer require registration with ECHA before being placed
on the EU market. Joint submission via SIEF (Substance
Information Exchange Forum) required for same substance from
multiple registrants.

Substances in articles — manufacturer / importer of articles
shall register substances intended to be released from articles
≥1 t/y under normal/reasonably-foreseeable conditions. SVHC
candidate substances in articles >0.1% w/w + >1 t/y require
notification per Article 7(2). Communication obligation per
Article 33.

Registration dossier content — technical dossier per Annex VI
structure + tonnage-band-specific information per Annexes
VII-X. Annex VII (≥1 t/y baseline) → Annex VIII (≥10 t/y adds
sub-acute toxicity) → Annex IX (≥100 t/y adds 90-day
repeat-dose + reproductive screening + chronic ecotox) →
Annex X (≥1000 t/y adds carcinogenicity + multi-generation
reproductive + chronic toxicity).

Chemical Safety Report (CSR) — required for substances ≥10
tonnes/year per registrant. CSR per Annex I includes: human
health hazard assessment (DNEL); environmental hazard
assessment (PNEC); PBT + vPvB assessment per Annex XIII;
exposure assessment (when classified hazardous OR PBT/vPvB);
risk characterisation (RCR = exposure / DNEL or PEC/PNEC; <1
= controlled risk).

Safety Data Sheet — required for hazardous substances +
mixtures placed on EU market. 16-section format per Annex II
(GHS-harmonised). Languages: official language of each Member
State where placed on market. Updated promptly on new hazard
information + authorisation + restriction + change requiring
exposure scenario update. Recipients receive updated SDS free
of charge for substances supplied in preceding 12 months.

Supply-chain communication — supplier of article containing
SVHC (candidate list per Article 59) at >0.1% w/w shall
provide recipient with information sufficient for safe use
(at minimum the substance name). Consumer request gets
response within 45 days. ECHA SCIP database notification per
Waste Framework Directive (EU) 2018/851.

Downstream user obligations — DU using substances/mixtures in
industrial / professional activities shall (i) apply
operational conditions + risk management measures per the
registrant's exposure scenarios, OR (ii) prepare own DU
Chemical Safety Report per Article 37(4) if outside the
registrant's exposure scenarios, OR (iii) report use to ECHA
per Article 38 if outside scenarios.

Authorisation — SVHC listed on Annex XIV cannot be placed on
the market or used after the sunset date without an
authorisation from the European Commission. Application for
authorisation per Article 60 includes: chemical safety
report; analysis of alternatives; substitution plan; socio-
economic analysis. Each downstream user using authorised
substance must notify ECHA within 3 months.

Restrictions — Annex XVII lists substances + mixtures + articles
subject to restriction on manufacture, placing on market, or
use (e.g., asbestos prohibition; PFOA + related; phthalates
DEHP/BBP/DBP/DIBP in articles; lead in jewellery). Restrictions
enforced at Member State level.

Self-classification + label + package obligation — manufacturer
/ importer / downstream user / distributor placing a substance
or mixture on the EU market shall classify it per CLP +
apply CLP-compliant label + packaging before placing on market.

C&L Inventory notification — substances subject to REACH
registration OR substances classified as hazardous + placed
on EU market shall be notified to ECHA C&L Inventory within
one month of being placed on market. Notifications
consolidated per substance; ECHA encourages harmonised
multi-notifier classification.

Harmonised Classification + Labelling (CLH) — substances with
Annex VI entry have mandatory classification for the listed
hazard endpoints. Self-classification supersedes only for
endpoints not covered by CLH. RAC opinions drive CLH additions.

Unique Formula Identifier (UFI) + Poison Centre Notification
(PCN) — mixtures classified for health/physical hazards
require UFI on the label + PCN submission to the PCN portal.
Consumer + professional uses compliance effective 2021;
industrial use compliance effective 2024.

Hazard classification system — physical (Part 2: 17 classes),
health (Part 3: 10 classes), environmental (Part 4: 2 classes).
Each class has categories with criteria for assignment. Building
blocks adopted variably by jurisdictions; CLP + OSHA HCS adopt
the core but with regional additions (CLP EUH + OSHA additions).

16-section SDS format — globally harmonised. Sections 1-16
cover identification, hazards, composition, first aid, fire,
release, handling, exposure controls, physical-chemical,
stability, toxicology, ecology, disposal, transport,
regulatory, other information.

Label elements — pictograms (9 standard pictograms);
signal word (Danger or Warning); H-statements per hazard +
category; P-statements selected per hazard. Color-coded
pictogram borders vary by jurisdiction (EU red; UN black/white).

Test facility organisation + personnel — Test Facility
Management responsibility; Study Director primary
responsibility per study; Principal Investigator(s) for
multi-site studies; Quality Assurance independent of study
conduct; documented qualifications + training for all
personnel.

Standard Operating Procedures — written approved SOPs for
all routine activities. SOPs available at workstation.
Deviations documented in raw data with reason + Study
Director acknowledgement. SOP revisions controlled per
organisation document-control SOP.

Study Plan (Principle 8.1) before study initiation; raw data
captured directly + promptly + legibly + signed + dated;
Final Report (Principle 9.1) reflects raw data + includes
QA Statement + archiving statement; archive (Principle 9.2)
retains Study Plan + raw data + specimens + Final Report +
QA records + SOPs at versions used; minimum 10-year retention
typical for chemical industry.

Pre-Manufacture Notice (PMN) — manufacturer / importer of a
NEW chemical substance (not on TSCA Inventory) shall submit
PMN to EPA at least 90 days before manufacturing or importing.
EPA reviews; may issue order requiring testing OR Significant
New Use Rule (SNUR) under Section 5(a)(2); may add substance
to Inventory with restrictions.

Existing chemical risk evaluation + restriction — Lautenberg
Amendments (2016) require EPA to systematically evaluate
existing TSCA Inventory chemicals; high-priority substances
undergo risk evaluation; restrictions imposed when unreasonable
risk identified (e.g., asbestos, methylene chloride
restrictions). EPA Risk Management Rule final actions.

Chemical Data Reporting (CDR) — every 4 years (next 2024
submission period for 2020-2023 data; subsequent every 4
years thereafter), manufacturers + importers report
production/import volumes + sites + processing/use information
for substances exceeding reporting thresholds. PFAS-specific
reporting per 40 CFR 705 (one-time 2024 PFAS reporting rule).

Import + export of TSCA chemicals — importers must comply
with TSCA at the point of import; export notifications
required for substances subject to certain regulatory
actions per Section 12(b). Certification at import +
compliance with Inventory + PMN obligations.

Policies for information security — defined, approved by management,
published, communicated to and acknowledged by relevant personnel
and interested parties, and reviewed at planned intervals or when
significant changes occur.

Legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirements relevant
to information security shall be identified, documented, and kept
up to date. The organization's approach to meeting each shall be
defined.

Separation of development, test, and production environments —
including separation of duties where appropriate — to reduce the
risk of unauthorized access or unauthorized changes to the
operational environment.

Understanding the needs + expectations of interested parties —
determine relevant interested parties (regulators, neighboring
communities, customers, suppliers, workers, NGOs), their relevant
needs + expectations, and which of those become compliance
obligations.

Environmental policy — top management establishes + maintains
a policy appropriate to the purpose + context including the
nature + scale + environmental impacts of activities, products,
services. Includes commitments to protection of the environment
(incl. prevention of pollution + other commitments e.g.,
sustainable resource use, climate change mitigation +
adaptation, biodiversity), fulfillment of compliance
obligations, continual improvement of EMS to enhance
environmental performance.

Environmental aspects — identify aspects of activities, products,
services that can be controlled or influenced; determine
associated environmental impacts considering a lifecycle
perspective. Determine significant environmental aspects
using established criteria. Maintain documented information
of aspects + impacts + criteria + SEAs.

Compliance obligations — determine + have access to the
compliance obligations related to environmental aspects;
determine how these apply to the organization; take obligations
into account when establishing + implementing + maintaining +
continually improving the EMS.

Planning action — plan to take actions to address significant
environmental aspects + compliance obligations + risks +
opportunities identified per §6.1.1, and to evaluate the
effectiveness of these actions. Integration into EMS
processes per §6.1.1.

Environmental objectives + planning to achieve them — establish
at relevant functions + levels, consistent with environmental
policy, considering SEAs + compliance obligations + risks +
opportunities. Measurable, monitored, communicated, updated.

Communication — internal + external communications relevant to
the EMS including: what, when, with whom, how. External
communication of significant environmental information as
established by compliance obligations + the communication
process. Responsiveness to relevant communications received.

Operational planning + control — establish + implement +
control + maintain processes needed to meet EMS requirements
+ implement actions identified in §6.1 + §6.2. Includes
operational criteria for SEAs, control of planned changes,
review of unintended changes + mitigation of adverse effects,
control / influence of outsourced processes, lifecycle
perspective in design + procurement.

Emergency preparedness + response — establish + implement +
maintain processes needed to prepare for + respond to potential
emergency situations identified in §6.1.1. Periodic test of
planned response actions where practicable. Periodic review +
revision based on test results + actual occurrences.

Evaluation of compliance — establish + implement + maintain
processes needed to evaluate fulfillment of compliance
obligations. Determine frequency, evaluate compliance + take
action if needed, maintain knowledge + understanding of
compliance status. Documented information retained as
evidence of evaluation results.

Nonconformity + corrective action — react to nonconformity
including taking action to control + correct it + deal with
consequences (including mitigating adverse environmental
impacts); evaluate need for action to eliminate causes;
implement; review effectiveness; make changes to EMS if
necessary.

Understanding the needs + expectations of workers + other
interested parties — determine + monitor interested parties
(workers, contractors, suppliers, customers, visitors,
regulators, communities, families of workers), their relevant
needs + expectations, which become compliance obligations.

OH&S policy — top management establishes + implements +
maintains a policy that includes commitment to: provide safe
+ healthy working conditions for prevention of work-related
injury + ill-health, appropriate to purpose + size + context
and the specific nature of OH&S risks + opportunities;
provide framework for setting OH&S objectives; fulfil legal
+ other requirements; eliminate hazards + reduce OH&S risks;
continual improvement of OHSMS; consultation + participation
of workers + their representatives.

Consultation + participation of workers — establish + implement
+ maintain processes for consultation + participation of
non-managerial workers (and their representatives where they
exist) in development + planning + implementation + performance
evaluation + actions for improvement of the OHSMS. Provide
mechanisms + time + training + resources; remove + minimize
barriers; specific topics requiring consultation OR
participation are listed in §5.4 a) and b).

Hazard identification + assessment of risks + opportunities —
establish + implement + maintain a hazard identification process
ongoing + proactive. Consider routine + non-routine activities,
workplace, work organization, factors affecting workers
(incl. psychosocial), past relevant incidents, emergency
situations. Assess OH&S risks + identify other risks to the
OHSMS. Identify OH&S opportunities + other opportunities.

Determination of legal + other requirements — determine + have
access to up-to-date legal + other requirements applicable to
hazards + OH&S risks + OHSMS; determine how these requirements
apply + need to be communicated; take into account when
establishing + implementing + maintaining + improving OHSMS.

Planning action — plan to take actions to address risks +
opportunities, address legal + other requirements, prepare
for + respond to emergency situations. Integrate into OHSMS
processes + other business processes. Evaluate effectiveness.

Awareness — workers shall be made aware of the OH&S policy +
objectives, their contribution to OHSMS effectiveness,
implications + consequences of not conforming to OHSMS
requirements, incidents + outcomes of investigations
relevant to them, hazards + OH&S risks + actions
determined relevant to them, ability to remove themselves
from work situations they consider to present an imminent
+ serious danger to their life or health, and arrangements
for protecting them from undue consequences for doing so.

Eliminating hazards + reducing OH&S risks — establish +
implement + maintain a process(es) for the elimination of
hazards + reduction of OH&S risks using the hierarchy of
controls: eliminate the hazard; substitute with less
hazardous processes / operations / materials / equipment;
use engineering controls + reorganization of work;
administrative controls including training; PPE. PPE is
the last resort.

Management of change — establish process(es) for implementation
+ control of planned temporary + permanent changes that
affect OH&S performance (new / modified products / services /
processes; workplace / surroundings / work organization /
working conditions; equipment; workforce; legal + other
requirements; knowledge / information about hazards + OH&S
risks; technology development). Review consequences of
unintended changes + mitigate adverse effects.

Procurement — establish process(es) to control procurement of
products + services so they conform to OHSMS. Includes
coordinating procurement processes with contractors to identify
hazards + assess + control OH&S risks arising from contractors'
activities + operations that impact organization OR workers OR
other interested parties.

Emergency preparedness + response — establish + implement +
maintain process(es) needed to prepare for + respond to
potential emergency situations identified in §6.1.2.1.
Planned response, training, communication of relevant
information to workers + interested parties, periodic testing
+ revision, evaluation + revision after testing + occurrence.

Incident + nonconformity + corrective action — react in a
timely manner to incidents + nonconformities including
controlling + correcting them, dealing with consequences;
evaluate (with participation of workers + involvement of
other relevant interested parties) the need for corrective
action to eliminate root cause(s); review existing
OH&S risk assessments + other risks; determine + implement
action needed including corrective; review effectiveness;
make changes to OHSMS if necessary.

8 risk management principles — integrated (part of all
activities), structured + comprehensive, customized (tailored
to org context), inclusive (stakeholder engagement), dynamic
(responsive to change), best available information, human +
cultural factors, continual improvement.

Risk management framework — leadership + commitment +
integration into governance + design + implementation +
evaluation + improvement of the framework itself. Distinct
from the risk management PROCESS (§6) which is the operational
execution.

Risk management process — communication + consultation; scope
+ context + criteria; risk assessment (identification +
analysis + evaluation); risk treatment; monitoring + review;
recording + reporting. Iterative across the lifecycle.

Integration — risk management is integrated into ALL
organizational activities + functions. Not a separate
function; embedded in strategy + governance + decision-
making + operations. ISO 31000 + ISO 31010 (risk assessment
techniques) together provide the meta-framework supporting
domain-specific risk standards (ICH Q9 / HARA / TARA /
HACCP / etc.).
